items.title: Kernel Adaptive Memory: testing persistent kernel memory for sequence models
items.subtitle: A falsification-first research program asking whether a kernel-routed bank of persistent supports adds anything to a sequence model — first as radial attention, now as a sparse, top-K-routed memory branch inside a standard decoder.
items.imgAlt: Diagram of the Phase I Kernel Adaptive Memory model: a sequence feeds radial context attention and a learned persistent support bank before a residual readout with optional online NLMS adaptation.
items.desc: Six phases of preregistered experiments asking whether a kernel-routed persistent memory helps sequence models: no general advantage yet, but the hypothesis has narrowed from dense radial attention to sparse, top-K-routed separable memory.

details.overview: Kernel Adaptive Memory (KAM) started as a bridge between kernel least-mean-squares methods, which predict with localized basis functions and admit cheap online updates, and transformers, which learn context-dependent routing. The original question was whether a learned radial geometry plus a finite bank of persistent supports could replace dot-product attention. Six experiment phases later, that broad claim is not supported; what survived is a narrower hypothesis about a sparse, top-K-routed memory branch that complements attention, and a research process designed so that a negative result is as usable as a positive one.
details.status: Active research program; six experiment phases through August 2026, Phases III–VI run on UF HiPerGator; no promotion decision yet.
what_i_built: The Phase I reference model: radial kernel context attention, a learned bank of persistent support keys and values, and an optional normalized-LMS readout, with seven matched command-line variants and four task generators (copy, hidden-regime grammar, Mackey–Glass, character text).

The Phase VI sparse separable memory layer: a standalone modern causal decoder (RMSNorm, SwiGLU) whose blocks can add a top-K kernel-routed memory branch of locally affine or low-rank experts behind a zero-initialized gate, plus widened-transformer, memory-token, mixture-of-experts, and product-key-memory controls at matched parameters.

A separable optimization surface: ridge and streaming recursive-least-squares solves for the expert values, alternating algebra/geometry schedules (8:1, 32:1, 128:1), trust-region rollback for geometry steps, and variable-projection test fixtures.
Manifest-driven, content-addressed, resumable Slurm array campaigns for HiPerGator, with dependency-gated aggregation and report jobs so a campaign can be rerun row by row without duplicating work.

Preregistered validity gates and locked decision memos that fix the estimand, paired-seed bootstrap intervals, sign-flip randomization tests, Holm correction, and equivalence margins (±1 percent in the current Stage 1 memo) before any result is inspected.
Independent audit scripts for output identity, task/optimizer dispatch, finite metrics, alternating-schedule coverage, freeze integrity, and matched key/expert permutation invariance.
how_it_works: Inside each decoder block, the normalized residual stream is mapped to a routing coordinate z, and every one of the M support keys is scored with a radial kernel distance under a learned diagonal metric.
Only the top-K supports (K much smaller than M) are kept; their scores are softmax-normalized among themselves, so stored capacity grows with M while active expert compute grows only with K.
Each selected support owns a locally affine expert, A_i·u + b_i (or a low-rank version); the memory output is the routing-weighted sum of the selected expert outputs.
That output re-enters the residual stream through a zero-initialized gate, so an untrained memory branch reproduces the baseline transformer's outputs and has to earn its influence.

Parameters split into slow "geometry" (keys, query map, metric) and fast "algebra" (expert values). They can be trained jointly, alternated at fixed ratios, or with the geometry frozen for the last 20 percent of training.

Every configuration is compared against a plain transformer, a widened transformer, memory tokens, mixture-of-experts, and product-key memory at matched total or active parameters; a result that merely adds parameters does not count.

writeup.lead: Can a sequence model keep the useful parts of attention while giving persistent memory an explicit kernel geometry and a fast path to adaptation? After six experiment phases the honest answer is: not in the general form I first proposed, but a narrower version of the idea is still open.

sections.heading: The question
body: Kernel adaptive filters such as kernel least-mean-squares (KLMS) predict with a bank of localized basis functions centered on stored samples, and they adapt online with cheap coefficient updates. Transformers learn context-dependent query/key routing and are far more general, but their memory is a growing context window of pairwise comparisons. KAM asked whether the two could be combined: give a sequence model a finite bank of learned **persistent supports** with an explicit kernel geometry, and keep a fast linear path for adaptation after the data changes.

The July 2026 working note framed this as a falsifiable program rather than a result. It defined matched baselines, the diagnostics that would be reported, and the conditions under which the idea should be declared not worth pursuing. Most of what follows is the record of running that program and letting it narrow the claim.

sections.heading: Phase I: one kernel calculation, two memories
body: The first implementation replaced scaled dot-product attention with a radial kernel score: similarity is a distance in a learned feature space under a positive diagonal metric, rather than a dot product. The same operator is used in two roles. In context attention a token queries earlier tokens from its own sequence. In persistent-memory attention a token queries a finite learned bank of M support keys and values that is shared across all sequences.

Because one primitive serves both roles, the model can be ablated cleanly: drop the support bank, drop context attention, or swap the radial score for the familiar dot product while keeping everything else fixed. Seven command-line variants (the full KAM, kernel-only context, memory-only, a dot-product transformer, a dot-product hybrid with supports, a GRU, and an MLP) and four tasks make up the original grid.

breakdown.label: Context attention
breakdown.text: Causal retrieval from the current sequence with a radial score; an optional local window W tests whether bounded context is enough.

breakdown.label: Persistent supports
breakdown.text: A learned bank of M key/value pairs that any sequence can query, intended to hold reusable structure rather than another copy of the context.

breakdown.label: Adaptive readout
breakdown.text: After a Mackey–Glass delay shift, the feature extractor is frozen and only the scalar readout is updated with normalized least-mean-squares (NLMS).

figure.alt: Phase I Kernel Adaptive Memory architecture: tokens flow through radial context attention and a learned persistent support bank into a residual readout, with an optional online NLMS update.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — The Phase I model: one radial attention primitive used for local context and for a persistent support bank, with online adaptation confined to the readout.

sections.heading: What the first matched grid showed
body: The first grid was 45 runs: five attention variants, three tasks (copy, hidden-regime grammar, Mackey–Glass), three seeds. It did not show a general advantage for the kernel geometry. Dot-product attention won or tied on copy and regime grammar. On Mackey–Glass the full KAM beat the dot-product transformer, but the dot-product hybrid, which adds the same support bank to ordinary attention, beat KAM; the useful ingredient there was the memory bank, not the radial score. On Tiny Shakespeare the dot-product transformer reached lower perplexity (6.96 versus 7.41) in about half the runtime, and a KAM model trained on copy length 16 fell to 16.1 percent accuracy at length 32. KAM also carried roughly 1.3 times the parameters, so the comparison was not even parameter-matched.

One signal survived. After a Mackey–Glass delay shift, adapting only the scalar readout with NLMS cut post-shift mean squared error by 44.5 percent relative to the frozen readout, and by 55.8 percent late in the stream. That is the KLMS-style property the project set out to keep, and it pointed the follow-up toward memory for nonstationary streams rather than toward a new attention score.

Phases II through V then hardened the method more than the architecture. A five-seed paired grid (50 runs) found no Holm-corrected comparison whose confidence interval excluded zero. A 1,728-row development search on switching dynamics moved the program onto HiPerGator. A bounded data-regime screen was filed as diagnostic only, and a learned-versus-fixed-feature campaign introduced active-parameter matching to within 1 percent and machine-checked validity gates that must pass before any result is read.

sections.heading: Narrowing to sparse separable memory
body: The Phase VI brief opens by stating that the broad claim, that the dense KAM bank should replace transformer attention, is not supported. The remaining hypothesis is narrower: a transformer may benefit from a **sparse, support-derived memory** whose values can be solved or adapted quickly while its support geometry changes slowly. Attention keeps modeling context; the memory branch supplies selectively accessed local transformations.

Concretely, each decoder block maps its residual stream to a routing coordinate, scores all M support keys with a radial kernel distance, and keeps only the top K (with K much smaller than M). Each selected support owns a locally affine expert, and the routing-weighted sum of those experts re-enters the residual stream through a zero-initialized gate, so an untrained memory branch reproduces the baseline model exactly. Stored capacity scales with M; active expert compute scales with K. Routing cost is a separate question, which is why the router zoo includes exact, chunked, product-key, and approximate variants with recall measured against an exact reference.

"Separable" refers to two parameter classes on two timescales. The fast **algebra** (expert values) is linear given the routing and can be solved by ridge regression or streaming recursive least squares; the slow **geometry** (keys, query map, metric) is updated by gradient steps, alternated with the algebra at ratios such as 8:1 or 32:1, and in the registered lifecycle frozen for the last 20 percent of training so the final tuning happens against stable routing.

breakdown.label: T-KAM-F
breakdown.text: Fixed or data-centered keys: is useful geometry available without learning key positions at all?

breakdown.label: T-KAM-L
breakdown.text: Learned keys, optionally as a low-rank delta from initialization: does learned support placement help?

breakdown.label: T-KAM-ALT
breakdown.text: Alternating algebra/geometry updates: does timescale separation improve optimization?

breakdown.label: Controls
breakdown.text: A plain decoder (T0), a widened decoder (T-WIDE), learned memory tokens, mixture-of-experts, and product-key memory at matched total or active parameters.

figure.alt: Phase VI sparse separable memory: the residual stream is routed to the top-K of M support keys by kernel distance, each selected support applies a local affine expert, and the weighted sum re-enters the block through a zero-initialized gate; slow geometry and fast algebra are trained on separate timescales.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — The Phase VI memory branch: kernel routing to K of M supports, local affine experts, a zero-initialized gate, and a slow-geometry / fast-algebra split.

sections.heading: The falsification discipline
body: Running a single-person architecture idea for six phases invites wishful reading, so the process is built to resist it. From Phase IV on, every phase has an implementation brief, a handoff document that asks for critique of the next step, a decision memo with outcome-to-action rules written before results are inspected, and a reproducibility record; earlier phases have a subset of these. Campaigns are immutable JSONL manifests where one row is one independently rerunnable job, submitted as Slurm arrays on HiPerGator's NVIDIA L4 nodes, with aggregation and report jobs held behind dependency gates.

The training seed is the inferential unit. Comparisons are paired by exact seed identity and reported with bootstrap confidence intervals, sign-flip randomization tests, Holm correction within declared families, and two-one-sided equivalence tests with declared margins (±1 percent in the current Stage 1 decision memo), because a non-significant difference is not evidence of equivalence. Confirmation campaigns fix their sample size in advance from a planning effect deliberately smaller than the pilot effect, to protect against winner's curse, and forbid optional stopping or seed replacement.

Independent audits catch what the pipeline gets wrong, and they have. Phase VI Stage 1 was rerun after audits found a geometry-factor coverage gap and a task/optimizer dispatch defect; an overnight campaign's adaptation rows were reclassified when an audit showed the declared adapters were never dispatched; and the Phase 6.2 mechanism study, 168 rows at 50 million tokens each, completed training and then failed its own preregistered validity gate because CUDA top-K tie-breaking was not invariant to matched key/expert permutations. That defect was localized to late memory layers, reproduced on three L4 hosts and absent on CPU, fixed with an opt-in support-identity tie-breaker, checked with a locked 26-checkpoint replay and a 24-row pilot, and a fresh 168-row rerun was preregistered rather than patching the original campaign.

sections.heading: Where it stands
body: As of 2026-08-09 (the last commit), the repository holds the Phase I reference implementation, the Phase VI decoder, memory, and optimization packages, and the campaign infrastructure, with 109 tests across all phases. On HiPerGator, Phase VI's Stage 0 correctness gate passed 128/128 rows, the corrected Stage 1 mechanism screen completed 3,000/3,000 rows with passing audits, and bounded Stage 2 through 6 profiles completed and were audited as implementation and resource evidence only. In the Stage 3 router profile, exact, chunked, and product-key routers recovered the exact reference's top-K choices with recall of 0.993, 0.991, and 0.983; the approximate router managed 0.477.

The quality evidence is thin and honestly labeled. A three-seed overnight language-modeling pilot put the fixed-key variant's validation loss 30.4 percent below a widened transformer at the registered token checkpoint, but with n = 3 the paired permutation p-value was 0.25, and the corrected decision was to retain the result as diagnostic only. The 156-row confirmation that followed (30 TinyStories pairs and 24 Tiny Shakespeare pairs at 50 million tokens per row) is referred to in later planning documents as not having met its primary superiority gate; its full report is not in the repository, so I do not quote its numbers here. The Phase VI decision memo's standing verdict is that no promotion decision has been made.

The current thread is a mechanism study of what sparse memory actually learns, not another attempt to win a benchmark: whether learned keys beat fixed ones, whether freezing geometry late helps, and whether alternating updates matter, with checkpoint-reuse causal checks (support and layer deletion, permutation tests) required before any further scaling. The preregistered support-identity rerun is the next result; whether it launched and what it found is not recorded in the repository as of this writing.

faq.q: Does KAM beat a transformer?
faq.a: No general advantage has been established. The first matched grid favored dot-product attention on most tasks, and the one underpowered pilot that favored sparse KAM (three seeds, p = 0.25) was filed as diagnostic only. The follow-up confirmation is described in the repo's later documents as not meeting its primary gate. The program's decision memo still reads "no promotion decision."

faq.q: Why did the framing change from "transformer alternative"?
faq.a: Because the data said so. Replacing the attention score with a radial kernel did not help, but adding a persistent support bank did help on delayed dynamics, and the online-adapted readout recovered much faster after a shift. The current design keeps standard attention for context and adds a sparse memory branch beside it, which is a complement rather than a replacement.

faq.q: What does "separable" mean here?
faq.a: The memory has two parameter classes. The expert values (the "algebra") are linear given the routing and can be solved exactly or adapted online. The keys, query map, and metric (the "geometry") are updated slowly, alternated with the algebra, and frozen for the last 20 percent of training so final tuning happens against stable routing.

faq.q: Why so much process for a solo research project?
faq.a: Because a solo project has no reviewer to stop optimistic readings. Preregistered gates, decision memos written before results are seen, paired-seed statistics with multiplicity correction, and independent audits have already caught several defects that would otherwise have been reported as findings, including a CUDA top-K tie-ordering bug that invalidated a 168-row campaign.

faq.q: Is the online adaptation result still part of the story?
faq.a: Yes. The 44.5 percent post-shift error reduction from NLMS readout adaptation in Phase I is the single result that has held up, and Phase VI keeps a dedicated online-adaptation lane: its brief compares frozen, SGD-readout, NLMS, recursive-least-squares, memory-value, and local-expert adapters on predict-score-reveal-update streams, and the bounded Stage 4 profile ran eight adapter choices as a descriptive screen.

glossary.definition: Kernel Adaptive Memory: a research program on giving sequence models a kernel-routed bank of persistent supports; the name now refers to the sparse separable memory branch rather than the original radial-attention model.
A learned key (and its value or local expert) in a finite memory bank that any token from any sequence can be routed to.
Scoring all M supports by kernel distance but keeping only the K best-scoring ones per token, so active compute grows with K while stored capacity grows with M.
A memory whose fast linear parameters (expert values) and slow nonlinear parameters (keys, metric, query map) are trained on different timescales or by different solvers.
Normalized least-mean-squares: an online update for a linear readout that scales its step by the input's energy; used here to adapt after a distribution shift with the feature extractor frozen.
A machine-checked precondition (all rows complete, outputs identical to reference, finite metrics, permutation invariance) that must pass before a campaign's results may be interpreted at all.

items.title: Latent-signal classification with hierarchical dynamical systems
items.subtitle: Reproducible pipeline that infers compact latent trajectories from multichannel time-series signals and evaluates them for downstream classification.
items.imgAlt: Diagram: hidden states evolve over time and generate the observed multichannel signal.
items.desc: Pipeline that maps noisy multichannel time-series observations to compact latent trajectories with a Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System (HLDS), then evaluates those trajectories for classification, separability, and stability.

details.overview: I built a reproducible pipeline for a general signal-modeling problem: infer low-dimensional latent dynamics from noisy multichannel observations, then use those latent trajectories as inputs to a downstream classifier. The public description stays at the level of the model, evaluation protocol, and research artifacts.
what_i_built: A reproducible data pipeline (loading → cleaning → segmentation → feature preparation) that turns observed time-series signals into model-ready inputs.
Training and evaluation scripts for a Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System (HLDS) that infers hidden variables evolving over time.
Diagnostics and scoring outputs for latent-trajectory stability, prediction, and class separability.
Automated summaries and artifacts so runs can be audited and compared (configuration capture, standardized outputs, and plots).
how_it_works: Observed signals are cleaned, standardized, and aligned into consistent time windows.
The HLDS learns hidden variables and transition structure that explain how those observations evolve.
At inference time, learned parameters are fixed and a Kalman-style recursion produces latent trajectories for held-out sequences.
A downstream classifier evaluates whether those latent trajectories separate the labeled classes under the same evaluation protocol.
deliverables: Run folders with configs, logs, metrics, and plots.
A standardized summary table for comparing latent representations and classifiers across evaluation splits.
collaborators: Computational NeuroEngineering Lab (CNEL), University of Florida

writeup.lead: A state-space pipeline for turning noisy multichannel observations into latent trajectories that a classifier can evaluate.

sections.heading: The problem: classify structure that is not directly observed
body: In many time-series problems, labels describe a class or regime while the observations are high-dimensional, noisy measurements. The useful representation is not given directly; it is a latent trajectory that evolves over time. This project asks whether a compact dynamical representation can make downstream classification more stable and interpretable than treating every window as an independent feature vector.

The goal is deliberately narrow: learn latent states, then test whether those states separate classes under a fixed evaluation protocol. The public page focuses on that technical problem rather than the application that motivated it.

sections.heading: Why a hierarchical dynamical system?
body: A Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System (HLDS) separates three things that are easy to conflate in a generic sequence model: what is observed, what is hidden, and how the hidden variables evolve. The hierarchy lets a small set of higher-level states summarize lower-level dynamics, while the linear-Gaussian structure keeps inference inspectable and data-efficient.

That structure gives the project useful failure modes. An unstable latent trajectory, a poor reconstruction, or a class boundary that disappears under held-out inference points to a different problem than a classifier score moving without explanation.

figure.alt: Diagram of a hierarchical dynamical system: noisy observed signal channels are generated by a compact chain of latent states evolving over time.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — The state-space view: a compact chain of hidden states evolves over time and generates the observed multichannel signal.

sections.heading: Training and inference are separate
body: The HLDS runs in two clearly separated phases. During training, a dual-Kalman procedure alternates between inferring hidden states and updating model parameters over multiple passes. During inference, those parameters are frozen and a Kalman-style recursion produces the latent trajectory for a new sequence.
Keeping the phases separate prevents a subtle evaluation leak: the classifier receives encodings produced under fixed parameters rather than a representation quietly re-fit to each held-out sequence.

figure.alt: Two-phase hierarchical dynamical system: training learns parameters with a dual-Kalman loop, then inference freezes them and produces latent trajectories for a classifier.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — Training learns the dynamical parameters; inference freezes them and turns a new sequence into a latent trajectory for classification.

sections.heading: The pipeline around the model
body: Each experiment is a fixed sequence of stages so representation quality and classifier performance can be compared fairly:

breakdown.label: Preprocessing
breakdown.text: Clean, standardize, and align observed signals into consistent time windows.

breakdown.label: Training
breakdown.text: Fit HLDS transition and emission parameters with the dual-Kalman procedure.

breakdown.label: Latent inference
breakdown.text: Run the fixed model on held-out sequences to produce compact trajectories.

breakdown.label: Classification
breakdown.text: Evaluate whether the latent trajectories predict and separate the labeled classes.

breakdown.label: Diagnostics
breakdown.text: Check stability, reconstruction behavior, class separability, and run-to-run consistency.

sections.heading: Classification on latent trajectories
body: The classifier is intentionally downstream of the dynamical model. That makes it possible to ask two separate questions: did the HLDS learn a stable, useful representation, and do those representations contain information that separates the classes? Evaluation artifacts keep those questions visible instead of collapsing everything into one score.

sections.heading: Where it stands
body: The reproducible pipeline, HLDS training/inference phases, classifier evaluation, diagnostics, and standardized run artifacts are in place. The next iteration is continued comparison across evaluation splits and model settings, with attention to latent-state stability and out-of-sample separability.
The public claim is intentionally bounded: this is a general latent-signal classification framework. The source data and application context are not part of the public project description.

faq.q: What does latent signal mean here?
faq.a: It means a lower-dimensional trajectory inferred from observed time-series measurements. The trajectory is not measured directly; the dynamical model estimates it from the observations and their temporal structure.

faq.q: Why use a hierarchical dynamical system?
faq.a: The hierarchy lets higher-level states summarize lower-level dynamics, while the state-space formulation makes transitions, emissions, and inference steps inspectable.

faq.q: How does classification enter the pipeline?
faq.a: The HLDS produces a latent trajectory for each held-out sequence. A downstream classifier then tests whether those trajectories contain information that separates the labeled classes.

faq.q: Does this page report a benchmark result?
faq.a: No. It describes the model and evaluation framework without publishing application-specific data, results, or claims that would identify the underlying study.

glossary.definition: Hierarchical Linear Dynamical System: a state-space model that represents observations with layered hidden variables evolving over time.
A time-evolving sequence of hidden variables inferred from observed signals.
A model that explains observations using hidden variables plus rules for how those variables evolve over time.
How distinctly a representation supports distinguishing the labeled classes in an evaluation set.

items.title: Zebrafish neural imaging: event detection & source separation
items.subtitle: Signal-processing research for detecting brief neural events and separating activity from background, artifacts, and measurement noise in zebrafish imaging video.
items.imgAlt: Frame from a zebrafish neural imaging video.
items.desc: Research platform for zebrafish neural-imaging video: statistical event detection for voltage recordings and a calcium-imaging experiment program that separates activity from background, artifacts, and noise.

details.overview: The project began with high-frame-rate voltage-imaging videos and now includes a calcium-imaging source-separation track. Across both modalities, the practical challenge is the same: preserve biologically meaningful activity while distinguishing it from motion, background structure, measurement noise, and other bright but misleading signals.
what_i_built: Preprocessing and normalization routines for voltage- and calcium-imaging video.
Statistical event detectors and proposal generators that score pixels and regions over time.
Source-separation experiments spanning PCA, ICA, nonnegative factorization, spectral denoising, latent dynamics, and morphology-aware spatial features.
Nested evaluation and human-review tools that separate proposal coverage, candidate ranking, signal preservation, and scientific interpretation.
how_it_works: Preserve an immutable activity carrier instead of allowing a denoiser to silently redefine the scientific signal.
Compute bounded source-separation, spatial, spectral, and dynamical features as auxiliary evidence.
Generate candidate events, then rank them independently under fixed candidate budgets.
Audit detection recall together with amplitude, area, timing, morphology, candidate burden, and visual remainders.
details.status: Active research; source-separation methods are under gated evaluation.

writeup.lead: Neural imaging gives you video of activity — and the hard part is deciding what belongs to the biology, what belongs to the measurement, and what evidence is safe to trust.

sections.heading: The problem: brief events in noisy video
body: Voltage and calcium imaging record brightness changes that correspond, imperfectly and on different time scales, to neural activity. The events you care about are localized and low-contrast, sitting on top of photobleaching, motion, persistent anatomy, and sensor noise. A naive brightness threshold either drowns in candidates or misses real activity.
So the real task is not 'find bright spots' — it is 'decide, per pixel and per frame, whether a change is more surprising than the background should produce.'

sections.heading: Current research: source separation without erasing the signal
body: The newest experiment track asks whether source-separation and denoising methods can improve event discovery in spontaneous calcium-burst recordings without changing the amplitude, footprint, or timing of the activity we ultimately want to interpret.

The clearest result so far is architectural rather than a single winning model: quiet-field standardization and spatial context have mattered more than model depth. At a budget of 58 candidates per burst, nested single-feature selection recovered **58 of 79** known events, compared with **51 of 79** for the archived carrier. At tighter budgets of 20 and 40, however, the native standardized carrier still performed best.

That trade-off matters. Several PCA, ICA, factorization, spectral, and state-space methods reduced noise or improved ranking, but none simultaneously passed the full preservation audit. The working design therefore keeps the activity carrier intact, uses separation outputs as bounded auxiliary evidence, and ranks candidates with a separate score.
[Read the experiment note →](../notes/source-separation-for-zebrafish-calcium-imaging.html)

breakdown.label: Preserve
breakdown.text: Keep an immutable activity carrier for scientific traces, timing, and downstream interpretation.

breakdown.label: Separate
breakdown.text: Use spatial, spectral, ICA, factorization, and dynamical channels as bounded auxiliary features.

breakdown.label: Rank
breakdown.text: Compare candidate ordering at fixed budgets instead of treating a larger candidate list as better precision.

breakdown.label: Gate
breakdown.text: Advance only when detection improves without unacceptable amplitude, area, timing, morphology, or stability loss.

sections.heading: Borrowing from radar
body: The detectors here come from radar signal processing, where the same problem — spot a faint target against a fluctuating background — has decades of theory behind it. I use CFAR-style adaptive thresholding to hold the false-alarm rate stable as the background changes, and a Quadratic Gamma Discriminator to flag deviations from a learned noise model.
Treating a microscopy problem as a detection problem is the whole idea: it means the thresholds adapt instead of being hand-tuned per recording.

figure.alt: A pixel intensity trace over time with an estimated noise band and an adaptive CFAR threshold; one spike crosses the threshold and is marked as a detected event.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — Per-pixel detection: the CFAR threshold adapts to the local noise band, so only a change that is genuinely unlikely — not merely bright — is flagged as an event.

sections.heading: The detection pipeline
body: Detection is built as a set of interchangeable stages so the pre-processing filter and the detector can be swapped and tuned independently. A parallel grid search runs across filter and detector parameters, and the best operating points are chosen by real detection-theory metrics rather than by eye.

breakdown.label: Pre-process (swap)
breakdown.text: A Gamma spatio-temporal filter for enhancement, or Kalman–MCC for robust background estimation via maximum correntropy — chosen per recording.

breakdown.label: Detect
breakdown.text: A CFAR detector scores each pixel/region over time and surfaces candidate events.

breakdown.label: Evaluate + select
breakdown.text: FROC (true-positive rate vs. false positives per image) and truncated AUC to compare detectors across the search, then top-K model summaries.

breakdown.label: Report
breakdown.text: Per-model diagnostics: event-duration histograms, FROC curves, sensitivity heatmaps, PSD comparisons, and qualitative montages.

figure.alt: Imaging video passes through an interchangeable pre-processing filter (Gamma ST or Kalman-MCC), a CFAR detector, evaluation by FROC and truncated AUC, and report generation; a parallel grid search spans the filter and detector, and a human review workbench feeds corrections back in.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — The grid-search detection pipeline. Filters and detectors are interchangeable, model selection uses detection-theory metrics, and a human review workbench closes the loop.

sections.heading: Keeping a human in the loop
body: Detectors are only half the system. A separate review workbench (a Fiji/Groovy plus browser workflow) lets a scientist inspect regions of interest and events with zoom, contrast, and overlay controls, accept/reject/mark-unsure at both the ROI and event level, and see a robust Kalman baseline under each trace. Decisions autosave, and ROI and event tables export for downstream analysis — so human judgment feeds back into which parameters win.

sections.heading: Modeling activity on a template grid
body: Beyond detection, a template-aligned 32×32 grid workflow models zebrafish left / right / neutral activity end to end: a grid autoencoder compresses each frame, a GRU predicts the latent code forward in time, and a classifier reads those latent codes — all with video-level splits so evaluation never leaks across a recording.

faq.q: What is CFAR?
faq.a: Constant False Alarm Rate: a family of adaptive thresholding methods that keep false detections stable across changing noise. It is a workhorse of radar detection.

faq.q: What is Kalman–MCC?
faq.a: A background estimator that uses the maximum correntropy criterion instead of plain least squares, which makes it robust to the heavy-tailed noise and outliers common in imaging video.

faq.q: How are detectors compared fairly?
faq.a: By detection-theory metrics rather than a single accuracy number: FROC curves and truncated AUC compared across a parallel grid search, instead of a single threshold picked by eye.

faq.q: Does this run in real time?
faq.a: It is offline analysis today, built for careful review and reproducible reports, with GPU acceleration where it helps.

faq.q: Has source separation solved the detection problem?
faq.a: Not yet. Some methods reduce noise or improve fixed-budget ranking, but no source-separation lane has passed every preservation and detection gate. The current evidence supports using separation outputs as auxiliary evidence while keeping the original activity carrier intact.

glossary.definition: A microscopy method that records fast changes related to electrical activity as video.
Constant False Alarm Rate: a family of adaptive thresholding methods that aim to keep false detections stable across changing noise.
Quadratic Gamma Discriminator: a statistical detector designed to highlight deviations from a learned background/noise model.
A family of methods that decomposes an observed recording into candidate sources such as neural activity, background structure, artifacts, and measurement noise.
The fraction of known events recovered when every method is allowed the same number of ranked candidates.

items.title: Time-series ML experiment library
items.subtitle: Reusable infrastructure for running, tracking, and comparing time-series machine learning experiments with consistent reporting.
items.imgAlt: Diagram of one experiment run: a config and one command produce an auditable run folder with a config snapshot, metrics, logs, and plots.
items.desc: Reusable experiment scaffolding for time-series ML: standardized configs, runs, metrics, and plots so model comparisons are fair and repeatable.

details.overview: Across projects, the same problem kept repeating: experiments become hard to reproduce once there are many datasets, models, and hyperparameters. This library is a practical solution: a consistent way to launch experiments, capture configuration, compute metrics, and export results.
what_i_built: A consistent ‘run’ layout (configs, outputs, plots) so results are auditable.
Utilities for sweeping model variants and hyperparameters in a controlled way.
Standardized metrics and plotting helpers for time-series tasks.
Performance-focused utilities (including GPU acceleration where appropriate) to keep iteration cycles short.
deliverables: One-command experiment runs that produce comparable outputs.
Reusable plotting and reporting utilities for papers and internal reviews.
details.status: Ongoing; shared across multiple research threads.

writeup.lead: The least glamorous project I have built, and the one that makes every other one reproducible.

sections.heading: Why build experiment infrastructure?
body: The same failure kept happening across projects: three months in, with a dozen datasets, several model variants, and a wall of hyperparameters, nobody can say exactly how a given plot was produced. This library exists to make that situation impossible.
It is a deliberately boring piece of software, and that is the point — reproducibility is not a feature you add at the end, it is a constraint you build in from the first run.

sections.heading: What a run looks like
body: Every experiment is one command that produces a self-contained run folder: the exact config that generated it, logs, computed metrics, and plots, all in a standardized layout. Two runs are always comparable because they were produced the same way, not because someone remembered to keep them consistent.

figure.alt: A config file feeds one command that produces a standardized, auditable run folder of config, logs, metrics, and plots, which makes two runs directly comparable.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — One config, one command, one auditable run folder — which is what makes comparing run A against run B honest rather than approximate.

sections.heading: A library of models behind one harness
body: The infrastructure grew out of a concrete need: comparing very different model families on the same time-series problem without the comparison quietly cheating. So alongside the run harness there is a library of adaptive and kernel filters, plus a configurable neural-network toolkit, all driven through one experiment runner.

Because every model is invoked the same way, a kernel adaptive filter and a neural network are held to identical signals and identical metrics — which is the only way a comparison between them means anything.

breakdown.label: Kernel adaptive filters
breakdown.text: QKLMS, KRLS, KRR, and Gaussian-process regression for nonlinear prediction.

breakdown.label: Functional / Wiener
breakdown.text: Functional Wiener (FWF / FWFE), the Functional Kalman Filter (FKF), ASLM, and a Wiener-filter baseline.

breakdown.label: Configurable NNs
breakdown.text: A hyperparameter-search toolkit including an information-theoretic stacked auto-encoder, run on GPU / HiPerGator.

figure.alt: Two model families — adaptive/kernel filters and configurable neural networks — feed a shared unified runner that evaluates them on benchmark chaotic signals and outputs comparable train/test MSE.
figure.caption: Figure 2 — Different model families, one harness: every model is benchmarked on the same signals with the same metric, so cross-family comparisons are honest.

sections.heading: Benchmarked on standard chaotic signals
body: Models are exercised on the classic nonlinear time-series benchmarks, where the right answer is known and difficulty is well understood:
bullets: **Mackey–Glass** — the standard delay-differential benchmark for nonlinear prediction.
**Lorenz** and **Hénon** — chaotic dynamical systems with known structure.
**Sunspot** — a real-world series for a sanity check against messy data.
Reported as **train / test MSE**, the same way for every model.

sections.heading: Design principles
body: Capture configuration; never trust memory. Standardize metrics and plotting so results line up across projects. And keep iteration fast — GPU acceleration where it helps — because infrastructure nobody wants to use does not get used.

faq.q: Is this a framework like MLflow or Weights & Biases?
faq.a: No — it is lighter and research-oriented. It is a model library plus an experiment runner for time-series work, not a general tracking service, though nothing stops you pairing it with one.

faq.q: Why benchmark on chaotic signals like Mackey–Glass?
faq.a: They are the standard proving ground for nonlinear prediction: the dynamics are known and the difficulty is well characterized, so a model's error is interpretable rather than a mystery.

faq.q: Is it open source?
faq.a: The code is currently private research code rather than a released package.

items.title: Spike-train decoding with kernel least-mean-squares (KLMS)
items.subtitle: A from-scratch Python reproduction of a classic neural-decoding result: turning noisy spike trains into a continuous control signal with a kernel adaptive filter.
items.imgAlt: Bar chart of normalised mean-squared error for the spike-KLMS decoder against binned KLMS and binned GLM baselines.
items.desc: A faithful Python reproduction of Li et al. (IEEE MLSP 2011): a spike-time RKHS KLMS decoder that maps spike trains to micro-stimulation, benchmarked against binned KLMS and GLM baselines.

details.overview: This project reproduces the core results of a well-known neural-decoding paper — Li et al., 'An adaptive decoder from spike trains to micro-stimulation using kernel least-mean-squares (KLMS)', IEEE MLSP 2011 — from scratch in Python, so the method can be understood, tested, and built on rather than taken on faith.
what_i_built: A spike-time RKHS KLMS decoder built on the cross-intensity kernel, operating directly on spike times.
A spike-time kernel APA family (KAPA / KNLMS / affine projection) with a projection-order sweep.
Binned-data baselines for comparison: a Gaussian-RBF KLMS and a Poisson-log-link GLM.
Synthetic neural-response generation with biphasic stimulation pulses, plus NMSE scoring and reconstruction plots.
how_it_works: Represent each spike train in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space via a spike-time kernel.
Learn an adaptive decoder online with kernel least-mean-squares, updating on each sample.
Reconstruct the continuous command signal and score it by normalized mean-squared error (NMSE).
Compare the spike-time decoder against binned KLMS and GLM baselines on the same synthetic data.
details.status: Synthetic reproduction implemented; rat VPL–S1 dataset sourcing in progress.

writeup.lead: A small, honest project: take a classic neural-decoding paper and rebuild its results from scratch until the numbers line up.

sections.heading: Why reproduce a 2011 paper?
body: Kernel least-mean-squares decoding of spike trains is a foundational idea in neural interfaces, and the fastest way to really understand a method is to rebuild it until it reproduces the original numbers. This project reimplements Li et al. (IEEE MLSP 2011) in Python — decoder, baselines, synthetic data, and metrics — as a clean reference I can trust and extend.
It doubles as a proving ground for the kernel-adaptive-filtering tools I use elsewhere, on a problem where the right answer is already published.

sections.heading: How the decoder works
body: Spikes are events in time, not evenly-sampled numbers, so the decoder embeds each spike train in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space using a spike-time (cross-intensity) kernel. A kernel least-mean-squares filter then learns online — updating on each sample — to map that representation to the continuous micro-stimulation command, which is scored by normalized mean-squared error.

sections.heading: Reproducing the published results
body: The point of a reproduction is the numbers, so the synthetic benchmark from the paper is rebuilt and every model is scored the same way. The spike-time kernel decoder leads the binned baselines, matching the paper's reported targets:

breakdown.label: Spike-KLMS
breakdown.text: NMSE ≈ 0.13 — the spike-time RKHS decoder, and the best of the three.

breakdown.label: Binned-KLMS
breakdown.text: NMSE ≈ 0.27 — a Gaussian-RBF KLMS on binned counts.

breakdown.label: Binned-GLM
breakdown.text: NMSE ≈ 0.35 — a Poisson GLM baseline.

figure.alt: Bar chart of NMSE: Spike-KLMS about 0.13, Binned-KLMS about 0.27, Binned-GLM about 0.35 — lower is better, so the spike-time kernel decoder wins.
figure.caption: Figure 1 — Reproduced synthetic NMSE. Working directly with spike times beats binning them, as the original paper reported.

sections.heading: Where it stands
body: The synthetic reproduction is complete, including the kernel APA family and a projection-order sweep. The next step is sourcing the real rat VPL–S1 dataset used in the original study to move from synthetic validation to real recordings.

faq.q: What is KLMS?
faq.a: Kernel least-mean-squares: a least-mean-squares adaptive filter applied in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space, so it can learn nonlinear mappings online while staying simple and interpretable.

faq.q: Why work with spike times instead of binned counts?
faq.a: Binning throws away temporal precision. A spike-time kernel keeps it, and the reproduction shows that this is exactly why the spike-time decoder reaches a lower error than the binned baselines.

faq.q: Is this original research or a reproduction?
faq.a: It is a faithful reproduction of a published result, built to understand and extend the method. The original work is Li et al., IEEE MLSP 2011.

glossary.definition: Kernel least-mean-squares: an adaptive filter that learns nonlinear mappings online in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space.
The sequence of firing times of a neuron, treated here as events in continuous time.
Normalized mean-squared error: reconstruction error scaled by signal power, so lower is better.
Reproducing-kernel Hilbert space: the feature space a kernel implicitly maps data into.
